title: Sunrise Dermatology Group
topic: Turning an objection into a conversation
summary: Zee asks for a moment before introducing the reason for the call.
He acknowledges a past concern, then asks what actually went wrong.
He closes with a specific, low-pressure walkthrough with the office manager.
reflection: How would you respond to a prospect who says, ‘We tried this before and it didn’t work’?

transcript.speaker: Zee
transcript.text: Hi, Doctor Ruiz. This is Zee with TargetOne. Have I caught you with a minute? I wanted to learn how your team handles topical prescription coordination today.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Ruiz
transcript.text: A minute is fine, but we tried a different compounding partner before. It was slow, and patients kept calling our front desk.

transcript.speaker: Zee
transcript.text: That sounds frustrating for your team. When you say slow, was the main issue the pharmacy turnaround, shipping, or not knowing the status?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Ruiz
transcript.text: Mostly not knowing the status. Our staff spent a lot of time chasing updates, and I don't want to repeat that.

transcript.speaker: Zee
transcript.text: That makes sense. Before recommending anything, I'd like to show your office manager how status updates work and discuss what turnaround your practice needs. Would a short walkthrough be useful?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Ruiz
transcript.text: Possibly. Maria, our office manager, would be the right person to look at that first.

transcript.speaker: Zee
transcript.text: Great. Could we set aside fifteen minutes with Maria on Tuesday at ten? I'll focus on updates and the handoff to your team.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Ruiz
transcript.text: Tuesday at ten works. Send the invitation to the front desk, and I'll ask Maria to join.

questions.prompt: What was the prospect’s main concern?
options: The lack of status updates and extra work for staff
The length of the sales call
questions.explanation: Dr. Ruiz clarified that chasing updates created work for the front desk. Zee discovered the specific issue instead of assuming it was price or shipping.

questions.prompt: How did Zee respond to the initial objection?
options: He acknowledged the experience and asked a clarifying question
He promised that every prescription would ship the same day
questions.explanation: Acknowledging the frustration made space for a useful discovery question. Zee avoided unsupported promises.

questions.prompt: What made the next step effective?
options: The prospect agreed to buy immediately
Zee said he would call back sometime
They agreed on a time, the right participant, and a focused agenda
questions.explanation: The walkthrough had a clear owner, time, and purpose: Tuesday at ten with Maria, focused on status updates.

title: Metro Pain Management
topic: Discover the problem before you pitch
summary: Edrin opens with a question about the current process.
He follows the first answer to understand who owns the work.
He checks his understanding before suggesting a focused demo.
reflection: Write one follow-up question you would ask to understand this practice’s workflow better.

transcript.speaker: Edrin
transcript.text: Hello, Anna. This is Edrin from TargetOne. Thanks for making time. Could you walk me through what happens after a provider sends a prescription today?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: The prescription goes out, and then our nurses handle the follow-up calls. Sometimes the patient calls us before we have any update.

transcript.speaker: Edrin
transcript.text: And when an update is missing, who takes responsibility for finding it?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Usually one of our two nurses. They call the pharmacy between appointments, which takes time away from the patients here.

transcript.speaker: Edrin
transcript.text: How often is your team dealing with that kind of interruption?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Several times a day. The biggest problem is that we don't have one clear place to check what is happening.

transcript.speaker: Edrin
transcript.text: So the priority is a clear way to check status, with less chasing for the nursing team. Have I understood that correctly? If so, I can tailor a walkthrough to that workflow.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Exactly. Let's include our lead nurse in a walkthrough on Thursday afternoon. She can explain the process in more detail.

questions.prompt: Why was Edrin’s opening question useful?
options: It let the prospect explain the current workflow in their own words
questions.explanation: An open-ended process question revealed the workflow and the pain point without leading the prospect.

questions.prompt: Who was most affected by the current process?
questions.explanation: Anna described nurses chasing updates between appointments, taking their attention away from patients.

questions.prompt: What did Edrin do before proposing a walkthrough?
options: Summarized the need and checked that he understood it
questions.explanation: Checking the summary with Anna ensured the walkthrough would address a real priority.

title: Harbor Point Pharmacy
summary: Zee learns that handoffs matter more than more inbound inquiries.
He describes only the workflow relevant to that priority.
He checks whether that benefit is useful before asking for more time.
reflection: Describe the value of a clear handoff in one sentence, using the prospect’s own priorities.

transcript.speaker: Zee
transcript.text: Hi, James. Thanks for speaking with me. Before I tell you about TargetOne, what would you most like to improve about working with new practices?

transcript.speaker: James
transcript.text: We don't really need more inquiries. We need better information when a practice hands a request over to us.

transcript.speaker: Zee
transcript.text: What tends to be missing from that handoff?

transcript.speaker: James
transcript.text: The right contact person and what the practice expects next. Our team ends up calling back just to clarify those basics.

transcript.speaker: Zee
transcript.text: Understood. The workflow I'd like to walk through records the practice contact, their request, and the agreed next step in one place. The point would be a clearer handoff for your team.

transcript.speaker: James
transcript.text: That would be more useful than just receiving another list of contacts.

transcript.speaker: Zee
transcript.text: Would it help if we used a sample request from your process in a short demo? You could tell us whether the handoff includes what your team actually needs.

transcript.speaker: James
transcript.text: Yes. Send me an agenda, and let's look at it Friday morning with our operations lead.

questions.prompt: What did James want to improve?
options: The clarity of information in a practice handoff
The number of cold calls his team makes
questions.explanation: James explicitly prioritized complete handoff information over more inquiries.

questions.prompt: Which approach made the value pitch relevant?
options: Linking a clear contact and next step to fewer clarification calls
questions.explanation: Zee connected a specific workflow to the problem James had just described.

questions.prompt: Why propose using a sample request in the demo?
options: To let the team assess the workflow against their real needs
questions.explanation: Using an example from their process makes the discussion concrete and lets the prospect evaluate relevance.

title: Oak Street Pediatrics
topic: Earn time with a busy prospect
summary: Will respects that the prospect is between appointments.
He asks permission for one sentence and keeps it short.
He lets the prospect choose between two callback times.
reflection: Write a one-sentence opening for a prospect who only has 20 seconds.

transcript.speaker: Will
transcript.text: Hi, Doctor Chen. This is Will at TargetOne. Is this an okay time for a brief introduction?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Chen
transcript.text: Honestly, not really. I'm between appointments and have about twenty seconds.

transcript.speaker: Will
transcript.text: Of course. May I give you one sentence so you can decide whether a callback would be worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Chen
transcript.text: Go ahead.

transcript.speaker: Will
transcript.text: We help practice teams explore a clearer process for coordinating with their pharmacy partners, and I'd like to understand whether follow-up is an issue for your office.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Chen
transcript.text: It can be, but our office manager handles that. Call back when she is here.

transcript.speaker: Will
transcript.text: Thank you. Would tomorrow at nine or Wednesday at two be better for a quick call with your office manager?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Chen
transcript.text: Wednesday at two. Ask for Olivia. She can tell you whether it is relevant.

questions.prompt: What did Will do when the prospect said they were busy?
options: Asked permission for a one-sentence introduction
Told them the call was urgent
questions.explanation: Will acknowledged the time limit and requested permission for a very brief introduction.

questions.prompt: Who was the right person for the follow-up?
questions.explanation: Dr. Chen identified the office manager as the person responsible for the workflow.

questions.prompt: Which callback did they agree on?
questions.explanation: Will offered two specific times, and the prospect chose Wednesday at two.

title: Bayview Internal Medicine
summary: Will agrees to send information without pushing back.
He asks what would make the email useful to the prospect.
He gets permission for a specific follow-up after the email.
reflection: What question could you ask to make a ‘send me an email’ response more productive?

transcript.speaker: Will
transcript.text: Hi, Sarah. This is Will from TargetOne. I am calling about your practice's coordination with pharmacy partners. Do you have a moment?

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Could you just send me an email? I get a lot of calls and can't go through a presentation right now.

transcript.speaker: Will
transcript.text: Absolutely. To make it useful, is your main interest improving follow-up, understanding the setup process, or something else?

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: The setup process. We are a small team, and I can't take on another complicated implementation.

transcript.speaker: Will
transcript.text: Understood. I'll send a short outline of the setup steps and what we would need from your team, so you can judge the effort.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: That is fine. Please keep it brief and don't add me to a daily mailing list.

transcript.speaker: Will
transcript.text: Of course. I'll send the outline you requested. Would it be okay to follow up once on Thursday to see if there are questions?

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Thursday is okay. Email first, and I will let you know if a call makes sense.

questions.prompt: What information did Sarah actually want?
options: A full catalog of every service
A short outline of setup steps and team effort
questions.explanation: Sarah was concerned about implementation effort for her small team.

questions.prompt: What made Will’s follow-up question appropriate?
options: It helped tailor the email without forcing a presentation
It ignored the request to end the call
questions.explanation: Will accepted the email request and asked one focused question to make the information relevant.

questions.prompt: What follow-up did Sarah permit?
questions.explanation: Sarah allowed a Thursday follow-up by email and would decide whether a call was useful.

title: Lakeside Family Medicine
summary: Will acknowledges a successful existing partnership.
He explores whether anything falls outside its current scope.
He offers to assess a backup process without asking for a switch.
reflection: How would you uncover an opportunity without criticizing a prospect’s current partner?

transcript.speaker: Will
transcript.text: Hello, Michael. This is Will with TargetOne. I'd like to learn about how your office coordinates with its pharmacy partners.

transcript.speaker: Michael
transcript.text: We already have someone we work with, and we are happy with them. We are not looking to change.

transcript.speaker: Will
transcript.text: It's good that you have a relationship that works. I'm not asking you to change it. Is there anything outside their current scope that your team still has to solve separately?

transcript.speaker: Michael
transcript.text: Sometimes we need a backup contact when our usual person is away. That can slow us down.

transcript.speaker: Will
transcript.text: How does the team handle those situations now?

transcript.speaker: Michael
transcript.text: We call the main number and hope someone can help. It isn't a big enough problem to replace a partner over.

transcript.speaker: Will
transcript.text: That makes sense. Would a conversation focused only on a backup process be useful? We could first see whether there is anything we can help with, alongside your existing relationship.

transcript.speaker: Michael
transcript.text: I could give you ten minutes next week to discuss that. Please keep it focused on the backup process.

questions.prompt: How did Will handle the existing partnership?
options: He acknowledged the relationship and explored gaps in its scope
questions.explanation: Respecting a working relationship helped Will explore a specific unmet need.

questions.prompt: What gap did Michael identify?
options: A backup contact when their usual person is away
A need for a new office
questions.explanation: The occasional absence of their usual contact was the one issue Michael described.

questions.prompt: What should the next conversation focus on?
questions.explanation: Michael agreed to ten minutes specifically about a backup process.

title: Greenway Urgent Care
summary: Edrin treats the front desk contact as a helpful partner.
He asks who owns the process and how decisions are made.
He agrees on the preferred route for a relevant introduction.
reflection: Write a respectful question that helps you identify who owns a prospect’s decision process.

transcript.speaker: Edrin
transcript.text: Good morning. This is Edrin at TargetOne. Could you help me find the right person to speak with about pharmacy coordination for your clinics?

transcript.speaker: Reception
transcript.text: That might be our operations director, but she doesn't take unscheduled sales calls.

transcript.speaker: Edrin
transcript.text: I understand. What is the best way to share a short introduction with her?

transcript.speaker: Reception
transcript.text: You can email our general address. I forward relevant information to Priya, the director.

transcript.speaker: Edrin
transcript.text: Thank you. Does Priya manage this for all locations, or does each clinic make its own decision?

transcript.speaker: Reception
transcript.text: Priya reviews new processes for all three locations. She normally brings in the lead clinic manager after the initial review.

transcript.speaker: Edrin
transcript.text: That is helpful. I'll send a brief note explaining the workflow we would like to discuss, addressed to Priya. Is there a subject line that makes it easy for you to route?

transcript.speaker: Reception
transcript.text: Put pharmacy coordination, attention Priya, in the subject. I will send it to her, and she can reply if it is relevant.

questions.prompt: Who reviews new processes for the three clinics?
questions.explanation: The receptionist explained that Priya reviews processes across all three locations.

questions.prompt: Which action showed respect for the gatekeeper?
options: Asking for the preferred way to share an introduction
Pretending to be a personal friend
questions.explanation: Edrin respected the no-unscheduled-calls boundary and asked how to route relevant information.

questions.prompt: What was the agreed next step?
options: Email a short introduction with the requested subject line
questions.explanation: The receptionist gave a clear email route and subject line for Priya’s review.

title: Riverside Wellness Spa
topic: Respond to an early price question
summary: Zee acknowledges the budget question directly.
He avoids quoting an unsupported figure before understanding scope.
He agrees to provide a written scope and price for review.
reflection: How would you answer a pricing question when you do not yet know the required scope?

transcript.speaker: Zee
transcript.text: Hi, Emma. Thanks for your interest in TargetOne. What would you like to cover first?

transcript.speaker: Emma
transcript.text: Just tell me the price. We are watching our budget, so I don't want a long demo if it is out of reach.

transcript.speaker: Zee
transcript.text: That's a fair place to start. I don't want to give you an inaccurate number. May I ask two quick questions about the scope so I can get you the right pricing?

transcript.speaker: Emma
transcript.text: Okay, as long as this is quick.

transcript.speaker: Zee
transcript.text: Would this be for one location or several? And are you exploring just the coordination workflow, or support for your team's setup as well?

transcript.speaker: Emma
transcript.text: One location. We'd want to understand the setup support too. I need the full cost, not just a starting figure.

transcript.speaker: Zee
transcript.text: Understood. I'll get you a written breakdown for one location, including the requested setup support and any assumptions. You can review that before deciding whether to schedule a demo.

transcript.speaker: Emma
transcript.text: That works. Send the breakdown, and then we can decide if the next conversation makes sense.

questions.prompt: Why didn’t Zee quote a number immediately?
options: He wanted to ignore the budget
He needed the scope to avoid giving inaccurate pricing
He was offering the service for free
questions.explanation: Zee acknowledged the price question and explained that accurate pricing required two details about scope.

questions.prompt: What scope did Emma describe?
options: One location with setup support included in the breakdown
questions.explanation: Emma specified one location and asked to see the full cost including setup support.

questions.prompt: What should happen before scheduling the demo?
options: Emma should receive and review a written price breakdown
questions.explanation: The agreed step was a written breakdown so Emma could evaluate fit before committing more time.

title: Summit Orthopedic Partners
topic: Turn interest into a clear next step
summary: Edrin recaps the problem before asking for a meeting.
He includes both the process owner and the budget reviewer.
He confirms a time, an agenda, and what to prepare.
reflection: Write a closing question that includes a next action, the right people, and a specific time.

transcript.speaker: Edrin
transcript.text: Alex, based on what you've shared, your team wants a clearer handoff and fewer calls to find the right contact. Is that a fair summary?

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: Yes, that is the main issue. What you described sounds interesting. Send something over, and we will take a look.

transcript.speaker: Edrin
transcript.text: Happy to. To make the next step useful, would a twenty-minute walkthrough with the people involved be better than a general brochure? We could use a sample handoff from your team.

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: Maybe. Our practice administrator needs to be included if there is a cost involved.

transcript.speaker: Edrin
transcript.text: Absolutely. Who owns the day-to-day process and should also join?

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: That would be me. The administrator is Jordan. We are both usually free on Tuesday after two.

transcript.speaker: Edrin
transcript.text: Would Tuesday at two thirty work for you and Jordan? I'll send a twenty-minute invite with an agenda: your current handoff, a sample workflow, and questions about scope and cost.

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: Yes, send it for two thirty. I'll bring an example of a handoff that was difficult last week.

questions.prompt: Who should join the walkthrough?
options: Alex and Jordan, covering the workflow and budget
questions.explanation: Alex owns the process, while Jordan, the practice administrator, needs to review cost.

questions.prompt: What did they agree to prepare?
options: A sample difficult handoff from the team
questions.explanation: Alex offered to bring a real workflow example so the walkthrough could be specific.

questions.prompt: Which detail made the meeting commitment concrete?
options: ‘Let us know when you are free’
Tuesday at 2:30, for 20 minutes, with a defined agenda
questions.explanation: The participants, time, duration, and agenda were all clear at the end of the call.

title: Cedar Grove Medical Center
summary: Zee moves from a permission-based opening into discovery.
He explores the workload concern without promising effortless setup.
He closes with a small, relevant next step and clear ownership.
reflection: What are two techniques from these 10 demos that you will use on your first sales call?

transcript.speaker: Zee
transcript.text: Hi, Lisa. This is Zee at TargetOne. Have you got two minutes to see whether a conversation about your pharmacy coordination workflow would be useful?

transcript.speaker: Lisa
transcript.text: Two minutes is fine. We have a process already, but our front desk spends too much time chasing the status of requests.

transcript.speaker: Zee
transcript.text: When that happens, what information is the team usually trying to find?

transcript.speaker: Lisa
transcript.text: Who has the request and what is supposed to happen next. But I am worried that setting up another process will create even more work.

transcript.speaker: Zee
transcript.text: That is a reasonable concern. Any change takes effort, so I would want us to assess that honestly. Could we first map one typical request together and identify where the handoff breaks down?

transcript.speaker: Lisa
transcript.text: I could do that. I would need our front desk lead there because she knows the detail.

transcript.speaker: Zee
transcript.text: Great. How about Thursday at eleven for fifteen minutes with you and your front desk lead? I'll send a simple agenda. If you bring one example, we can look at the current process and then decide together whether another step is worthwhile.

transcript.speaker: Lisa
transcript.text: Thursday at eleven works. I'll invite the front desk lead and bring an example. Let's start there and see if it helps.

questions.prompt: What did Zee do when Lisa raised the setup concern?
options: Promised setup would take no effort
Acknowledged the concern and proposed assessing one workflow first
questions.explanation: Zee was honest that change takes effort and suggested a small step to assess whether it was worthwhile.

questions.prompt: Why include the front desk lead?
options: She knows the day-to-day process in detail
She must approve all sales calls
To make the meeting as large as possible
questions.explanation: Lisa said the front desk lead could explain the actual handoff details.

questions.prompt: Which description best captures the final agreement?
options: An open-ended promise to stay in touch
A short working session with clear preparation and a shared decision afterward
questions.explanation: Both sides had responsibilities: Zee would send the agenda, Lisa would bring an example and the right colleague, and they would evaluate the next step together.
